topic: The Haber process and the use of NPK fertilisers (chemistry only)
subject: chemistry

items.q: What is manufactured directly by the Haber process?
items.correct: Ammonia, which is then used to make nitrogen fertilisers
items.misconception: Ammonium nitrate, ready for spreading onto farm fields
items.why: The process is always introduced as 'how we feed the world', so students collapse the two steps into one. Ammonia is the product. Reacting it with nitric acid gives ammonium nitrate, and that is the fertiliser.
items.random_wrong: Nitric acid, which is sprayed on crops as plant feed

items.q: Which pair of gases are the raw materials for the Haber process?
items.correct: Nitrogen and hydrogen
items.misconception: Nitrogen and oxygen gas
items.why: Students remember 'nitrogen from the air' and assume the second gas must arrive the same way, and air does contain traces of hydrogen compounds as water vapour. Air is about 78% nitrogen but almost no hydrogen. The hydrogen is obtained from natural gas.
items.random_wrong: Hydrogen and methane

items.q: A student is asked to give a source of the nitrogen used in the Haber process. Which answer is correct?
items.correct: It is obtained from the air, which is about 78% nitrogen
items.misconception: It is obtained from natural gas, together with the hydrogen
items.why: Students remember 'nitrogen from the air' and assume the second gas must arrive the same way, and air does contain traces of hydrogen compounds as water vapour. Air is about 78% nitrogen but almost no hydrogen. The hydrogen is obtained from natural gas.
items.random_wrong: It is obtained by heating ammonium salts in large vessels

items.q: Which is the usual industrial source of the hydrogen used in the Haber process?
items.correct: Natural gas, which consists mainly of methane
items.misconception: Electrolysis of water, which splits it into elements
items.why: Electrolysis of water is the hydrogen source students meet first in class, so it is the one they recall. Electrolysis needs large amounts of electricity. Industry reacts methane from natural gas to obtain hydrogen.
items.random_wrong: The air, as hydrogen is one of the gases present in it

items.q: Which conditions are used in the Haber process?
items.correct: An iron catalyst, 450 degrees C and 200 atmospheres
items.misconception: An iron catalyst, 450 degrees C and 20 atmospheres
items.why: Students assume industry always picks the condition that maximises yield, ignoring the cost of the pipework. Yield keeps rising with pressure, so the limit is economic and about safety, not chemical.
items.random_wrong: A nickel catalyst, 450 degrees C and 200 atmospheres

items.q: What is the effect of the iron catalyst in the Haber process?
items.correct: It speeds up the rate at which the equilibrium is reached
items.misconception: It increases the yield of ammonia formed at equilibrium
items.why: 'Catalyst' is filed under 'makes the reaction better', and more ammonia per hour is confused with more ammonia at equilibrium. A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium arrives sooner but at the same position.
items.random_wrong: It is used up slowly and has to be replaced each time

items.q: The Haber reaction is reversible. What does this mean inside the reactor?
items.correct: Some of the ammonia breaks down into nitrogen and hydrogen
items.misconception: All the nitrogen and hydrogen react, then some ammonia breaks down
items.why: The double arrow is read as 'first one way, then the other' rather than as both happening together. Both directions happen at the same time in the reactor, which is why the ammonia has to be removed as it forms.
items.random_wrong: The reaction runs forwards during the day and backwards at night

items.q: Which equation for the Haber process is written as the specification gives it?
items.correct: nitrogen +hydrogen ⇌ammonia
items.misconception: ammonia ⇌nitrogen + hydrogen
items.why: Nearly every equation students have written before uses a single arrow, so it is the default. The specification writes nitrogen +hydrogen ⇌ ammonia. The double arrow is part of the chemistry.
items.random_wrong: nitrogen + hydrogen → ammonia

items.q: Which balanced symbol equation represents the Haber process?
items.misconception: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ NH3
items.why: Students balance the hydrogen but forget that two ammonia molecules are needed to use both nitrogen atoms. Two nitrogen atoms enter, so two NH3 molecules must leave. Check both elements before stopping.
items.random_wrong: N + 3H ⇌ NH3

items.q: The mixture leaving the reactor is cooled. What happens?
items.correct: The ammonia liquefies and is removed from the gas mixture
items.misconception: The nitrogen and the hydrogen liquefy and are then drawn off
items.why: Students know air can be liquefied to separate nitrogen, and transfer that to this reactor. Ammonia condenses at about -33 degrees C, far higher than nitrogen or hydrogen, so it is the one that turns liquid first.
items.random_wrong: All three gases liquefy together and are then distilled

items.q: What happens to the nitrogen and hydrogen that have not reacted?
items.correct: They are recycled back through the reactor
items.misconception: They are burnt to provide heat for the reactor
items.why: In laboratory work leftover reactants are simply discarded, so students carry that habit over to industry. Recycling the unreacted gases raises the overall conversion and avoids wasting expensive raw materials.
items.random_wrong: They are released into the air as harmless gases

items.q: A graph shows the rate of the Haber reaction against temperature at a fixed pressure. What does it show?
items.correct: The rate rises as the temperature is increased
items.misconception: The rate falls steadily as the temperature is increased
items.why: Students learn that yield falls with temperature and then read the rate axis as if it were a yield axis. Yield and rate respond to temperature in opposite ways. Check the axis label before describing the trend.
items.random_wrong: The rate is unchanged by temperature at constant pressure

items.q: A graph shows the percentage yield of ammonia against pressure at 450 degrees C. What is the trend, and why?
items.correct: Yield rises, because there are fewer gas molecules in the ammonia
items.misconception: Yield falls, because squashing the gases hinders the reaction
items.why: 'Squashing' is imagined as making the reaction harder rather than as favouring the side with fewer molecules. Four molecules of gas become two, so higher pressure shifts the equilibrium towards ammonia.
items.random_wrong: Yield is constant, because pressure only changes the rate

items.q: Inside a sealed Haber reactor at equilibrium, what is true?
items.correct: Both reactions are still going on at the same rate
items.misconception: Both the forward and reverse reactions have stopped
items.why: Nothing appears to change, and 'no change' is read as 'nothing is happening'. Equilibrium is dynamic: the forward and reverse reactions continue but cancel each other out.
items.random_wrong: The amounts of all three gases are now equal

items.q: Ammonia is removed from the mixture as it liquefies. What is the effect on the equilibrium?
items.correct: It shifts towards the ammonia side, so more gas reacts
items.misconception: There is no effect, since the ammonia has already been made
items.why: Students think of removal as happening after the chemistry, rather than as a change the system responds to. Taking a product out moves the equilibrium to replace it, which is why removal and recycling raise the overall conversion.
items.random_wrong: It shifts back towards the nitrogen and hydrogen instead

items.q: Why is the Haber process not run at a much lower temperature than 450 degrees C?
items.correct: Because the reaction would then be far too slow to use
items.misconception: Because the yield of ammonia would be lower at low temperatures
items.why: The exothermic argument is learned in isolation and applied without asking how long the plant would have to wait. A high yield reached too slowly is worth nothing. The temperature chosen trades yield for rate.
items.random_wrong: Because the iron catalyst does not work at all below 450 C

items.q: What is meant by the trade-off between rate of production and position of equilibrium?
items.correct: The conditions give the most ammonia per day, not the best yield or the fastest rate
items.misconception: The conditions chosen are simply those that give the fastest possible reaction
items.why: Rate is the more familiar idea, so the equilibrium half of the argument gets dropped. Both matter. A very hot reactor is fast but converts little; the compromise maximises production overall.
items.random_wrong: The conditions chosen are the ones giving the highest possible yield of ammonia

items.q: Why is a pressure of about 200 atmospheres used rather than a far higher one?
items.correct: Because stronger plant, more energy and greater risk cost more
items.misconception: Because a higher pressure would reduce the yield of the ammonia made
items.why: 'Squashing' is imagined as making the reaction harder rather than as favouring the side with fewer molecules. Four molecules of gas become two, so higher pressure shifts the equilibrium towards ammonia.
items.random_wrong: Because the iron catalyst is destroyed above 200 atmospheres

items.q: The nitrogen for the Haber process is taken from the air. Which reason best explains this choice?
items.correct: Air is free and is about 78% nitrogen, so it is the cheapest source
items.misconception: Nitrogen taken from the air is more reactive than nitrogen from a tank
items.why: Students look for a chemical reason when the reason is availability and cost. The specification links the conditions and raw materials to availability and cost. Air costs nothing to obtain.
items.random_wrong: Air already contains all the hydrogen that is needed for the reaction

items.q: An NPK fertiliser contains compounds of which three elements?
items.correct: Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium
items.misconception: Nitrogen, phosphorus and krypton, symbol K
items.why: K looks like it should belong to a word beginning with K, and potassium does not. K is the symbol for potassium, from its Latin name kalium. Krypton is Kr.
items.random_wrong: Nitrogen, potassium and carbon, from K

items.q: Why is an NPK fertiliser described as a formulation?
items.correct: Because it is a mixture of salts blended to give set percentages of N, P and K
items.misconception: Because it is one single compound whose formula contains all three elements
items.why: The single label NPK suggests a single substance with a single formula. No one salt supplies all three elements economically, so NPK fertilisers are mixtures made to a recipe.
items.random_wrong: Because its salts all dissolve to give exactly the same ions in the soil

items.q: Ammonia from the Haber process can be used to manufacture which substances?
items.correct: Ammonium salts and nitric acid
items.misconception: Ammonium salts and sulfuric acid
items.why: Sulfuric acid appears in the same fertiliser topic, so it gets attached to ammonia as well. Sulfuric acid is made from sulfur, not from ammonia. Ammonia gives ammonium salts and nitric acid.
items.random_wrong: Nitric acid and sulfuric acid

items.q: Which of these fertiliser raw materials are obtained by mining?
items.correct: Potassium chloride, potassium sulfate and phosphate rock
items.misconception: Ammonium nitrate, potassium sulfate and phosphate rock
items.why: Students expect every named salt in an industrial topic to be a manufactured product. Potassium chloride and potassium sulfate are mined, like phosphate rock. Unlike it, they are already suitable for use.
items.random_wrong: Potassium chloride and nitric acid, but not phosphate rock

items.q: Why can phosphate rock not be used directly as a fertiliser?
items.correct: Because the phosphate compounds in it do not dissolve
items.misconception: Because it is too acidic and would damage the roots of the crop
items.why: Students reason about run-off, which is a real problem, and conclude that insolubility must be desirable. Solubility is essential for uptake. Run-off is a separate drawback of soluble fertilisers, not a reason to use insoluble ones.
items.random_wrong: Because it contains far too little phosphorus to be of any use

items.q: Phosphate rock is treated with sulfuric acid. What is produced?
items.correct: Single superphosphate: calcium phosphate and calcium sulfate
items.misconception: Calcium sulfate only, with the phosphate left in the rock
items.why: Students track the sulfuric acid and forget that the phosphate has to end up somewhere as well. Both salts are present. The product is described as single superphosphate.
items.random_wrong: Calcium phosphate only, known as triple superphosphate

items.q: Phosphate rock is treated with nitric acid. Which products are formed?
items.correct: Phosphoric acid and calcium nitrate
items.misconception: Ammonium nitrate and calcium oxide
items.why: Ammonium nitrate is the fertiliser students know best, so it is offered whenever nitric acid appears. There is no ammonia in this step. Nitric acid on phosphate rock gives phosphoric acid and calcium nitrate.
items.random_wrong: Calcium phosphate and calcium sulfate

items.q: Which salt is produced when phosphate rock is treated with phosphoric acid?
items.correct: Calcium phosphate, called triple superphosphate
items.misconception: Calcium sulfate, the salt in single superphosphate
items.why: The two superphosphates are learned as a pair and their compositions get swapped. The sulfate only appears when sulfuric acid is used. Phosphoric acid leaves calcium phosphate alone.
items.random_wrong: Calcium phosphate mixed with some calcium sulfate

items.q: A student makes ammonium sulfate in the laboratory by titration and crystallisation. How does industrial production of the same salt differ?
items.correct: It runs continuously on a large scale, with reactants recycled
items.misconception: It uses different chemicals, because the laboratory acids are too weak
items.why: The same salt is made in both, so students assume the method must also be the same. Scale changes the method: continuous operation, recycled reactants and integrated plants have no laboratory equivalent.
items.random_wrong: It is carried out in exactly the same way, but with larger apparatus

items.q: In a Haber reactor at 200 atmospheres the rate of production is 9, 21 and 33 tonnes per hour at 350, 450 and 550 degrees C. The percentage yield at the same three temperatures is 55, 28 and 12. What do the data show?
items.correct: The rate rises with temperature while the yield falls
items.misconception: The yield rises with temperature and the rate falls
items.why: Students learn that yield falls with temperature and then read the rate axis as if it were a yield axis. Yield and rate respond to temperature in opposite ways. Check the axis label before describing the trend.
items.random_wrong: Both the rate and the yield fall at higher temperatures

items.q: At 450 degrees C the rate of ammonia production is 12 tonnes per hour at 100 atmospheres, 24 at 200 atmospheres and 45 at 400 atmospheres. What do these data show?
items.correct: Doubling the pressure roughly doubles the rate
items.misconception: The rate falls as the gases are squashed up
items.why: 'Squashing' is imagined as making the reaction harder rather than as favouring the side with fewer molecules. Four molecules of gas become two, so higher pressure shifts the equilibrium towards ammonia.
items.random_wrong: The rate stops rising beyond 200 atmospheres

items.q: Why is a temperature of about 450 degrees C used?
items.correct: 450 degrees C is a compromise: a hotter reactor is faster but gives a lower yield of ammonia.
items.misconception: 450 degrees C is used because it gives the greatest possible yield of ammonia.
items.why: Students assume the chosen condition must be the best one for yield, because that is what the plant is trying to maximise. The forward reaction is exothermic, so yield falls as temperature rises. 450 degrees C buys rate at the cost of yield.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the product of the Haber process ammonia or ammonium?
items.correct: Ammonia, NH3. Ammonium, NH4+, is the ion found in ammonium salts.
items.misconception: The Haber process makes ammonium.
items.why: The two words differ by two letters and both appear in this topic, so they are easily swapped. Ammonia is the neutral molecule made in the reactor. Ammonium ions only appear once ammonia reacts with an acid.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: At equilibrium, how do the amounts of reactants and products compare?
items.correct: They are constant, but not necessarily equal to one another.
items.misconception: There are equal amounts of nitrogen, hydrogen and ammonia.
items.why: 'Equilibrium' suggests 'balance', and balance is pictured as equal quantities on each side. Equal rates, not equal amounts. The position of equilibrium decides how much of each is present.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the iron catalyst used up during the Haber process?
items.correct: No. The catalyst is not used up, which is part of why it is economic.
items.misconception: The iron catalyst is used up and must be replaced with each batch.
items.why: Anything added to a reaction is assumed to be a reactant. A catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up, so one charge of iron lasts a long time.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can phosphate rock be spread on fields as it is?
items.correct: No. Its phosphate compounds are insoluble, so it must first be treated with an acid.
items.misconception: Phosphate rock is mined and spread straight onto fields as a phosphorus fertiliser.
items.why: Because the rock is mined ready-made, students see no reason for a further step. Plants take up dissolved ions, so the phosphate must be converted into soluble salts before it is any use.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How is an ammonium salt made from ammonia?
items.correct: Ammonia is reacted with an acid, for example nitric acid to give ammonium nitrate.
items.misconception: Ammonia is reacted with an alkali.
items.why: Ammonia solution is alkaline, so students mistakenly pair it with another alkali rather than with an acid. Ammonia behaves as a base here. Base plus acid gives a salt, so ammonia plus nitric acid gives ammonium nitrate.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification; section 4.10.4 The Haber process and the use of NPK fertilisers (chemistry only)
